In Lesson 5 we built a GLM step by step: we added variables, merged
categories and capped numeric variables, and we checked every step on
validation data. In this exercise we finish the job. We will choose a
set of predictors, prepare them in **one place** so that training and
validation data are treated identically, and compare the resulting
models with the ones from Lesson 5.

```{r cell_01, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r cell_02, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(statmod)
options(scipen = 5)

source("/cloud/project/Support/enforce_data_types.R")
source("/cloud/project/Support/rmse_group.R")
source("/cloud/project/Support/emb_chart_plotly.R")
source("/cloud/project/Support/get_vars.R")
source("/cloud/project/Support/compare_models.R")
```

### Data and the train / validation split

This is exactly the setup from Lesson 5 (same data, same predictors, same
seed), so we get the same training and validation rows as before.

```{r cell_03}
dt_pol_w_claims <- readRDS("/cloud/project/Data/dt_pol_w_claims_target.rds")

var_types <- c(
  Year = "category", Time_on_book = "number", Customer_Type = "category",
  D_age = "number", D_age_banded = "category", BonusMalus = "number",
  D_ZIP = "category", VEH_type = "category", Veh_type1 = "category",
  Veh_type2 = "category", VEH_brand = "category", Construct_year = "number",
  Capacity = "number", Nr_of_seats = "category", Sum_insured = "number"
)

dt_pol_w_claims <- dt_pol_w_claims |>
  enforce_data_types(var_types)

dt_pol_w_claims <- dt_pol_w_claims[complete.cases(dt_pol_w_claims[names(var_types)]), ]

set.seed(58742) # same seed as in Lesson 5

n_rows <- nrow(dt_pol_w_claims)
train_idx <- sample(n_rows, round(0.80 * n_rows)) # 80/20 split between train and valid

train <- dt_pol_w_claims[train_idx, ]
valid <- dt_pol_w_claims[-train_idx, ]
```

### Extreme losses in the target

The burning cost is the average loss per policy-year, so a single large
claim on a short policy produces a huge value. Let's look at the highest
values:

```{r cell_04}
train |>
  arrange(desc(Burning_Cost)) |>
  select(Time_Exposure, Ult_Loss, Burning_Cost) |>
  head(5)

summary(train$Burning_Cost)
```

A handful of such values can dominate the fit and the validation
metric. A common remedy is to **cap the large losses** at a high
percentile of the positive losses. We compute the cap on the **training**
data only and then apply the same cap to both datasets - validation data
must not influence how we prepare the training data.

```{r cell_05}
target_cap <- quantile(train$Burning_Cost[train$Burning_Cost > 0], 0.995)
target_cap

# how many rows are affected
sum(train$Burning_Cost > target_cap)
sum(valid$Burning_Cost > target_cap)
```

### One function for all feature engineering

In Lesson 5 we repeated every transformation twice (once for `train`,
once for `valid`). That is easy to get wrong - if the two copies differ
even slightly (a different cap, an extra band boundary), the model is
validated on a differently prepared dataset than the one it was trained
on. A safer pattern is to write the transformations **once**, as a
function, and apply it to both datasets.

We will start with what we already know from Lesson 5 (merging
vehicle types). The remaining variables are added in the following
sections, we just keep extending this function.

```{r cell_06}
add_features <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      # cap the extreme losses in the target
      Burning_Cost = pmin(Burning_Cost, target_cap),
      # Lesson 5: merge vehicle types with (almost) no exposure with the base category
      Veh_type2_merged = ifelse(Veh_type2 %in% c("", "OTHER", "TRACTOR"), "CAR", Veh_type2),
      # Lesson 5: cap the construction year
      Construct_year_capped = pmin(pmax(Construct_year, 2005), 2015)
    )
}

train <- add_features(train)
valid <- add_features(valid)
```

Our starting point is the final model from Lesson 5 and its simpler
version with the vehicle type only:

```{r cell_07}
model_l5 <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Construct_year_capped,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

model_veh <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

compare_models(list("L5 final" = model_l5, "Vehicle type" = model_veh), train, valid)
```

### Which variable next? BonusMalus

Let's look at one of the unfitted variables, `BonusMalus`. It is a
bonus-malus level of the driver: the lower the number, the worse the
claims history. The picture shows the actual burning cost against the
prediction of our model that does not include it yet.

```{r cell_08}
train$pred_veh <- predict(model_veh, train, type = "response")

emb_chart_plotly(
  model = NULL,
  x_var = "BonusMalus",
  dt.frm = train |> rename(pred = pred_veh)
) |>
  show()
```

The actual burning cost drops steeply as the BonusMalus level goes up,
but the fitted line is flat - the model has no information about the
bonus-malus history. This is exactly the situation where adding a
variable should help.

The first idea is to add `BonusMalus` as a number, which means one
multiplier per level:

```{r cell_09}
model_bm_num <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

emb_chart_plotly(model = model_bm_num, x_var = "BonusMalus") |>
  show()
```

The actual burning cost does not fall by a constant percentage per
level. It falls from level 1 onward, but the negative levels (the worst
claims history) are risky too, and level 0 has surprisingly *low* risk -
it breaks the trend completely. A single coefficient is a straight line
on the log scale and cannot follow this shape. This is the situation from
Lesson 5 where **banding** a numeric variable into categories helps. We
choose the bands from the shape of the actual line (each band should
contain levels with a similar actual burning cost) and make sure that
every band has reasonable exposure. Negative levels and level 0 get their
own bands, because their risk is very different from their neighbours.

We put the banding into our function, so that it is applied to both
datasets in the same way. To keep the code simple, `add_features()` now
contains all the transformations we need in this exercise (they are
explained step by step below):

```{r cell_10}
add_features <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      # cap the extreme losses in the target
      Burning_Cost = pmin(Burning_Cost, target_cap),
      # Lesson 5: merge vehicle types with (almost) no exposure with the base category
      Veh_type2_merged = ifelse(Veh_type2 %in% c("", "OTHER", "TRACTOR"), "CAR", Veh_type2),
      # Lesson 5: cap the construction year
      Construct_year_capped = pmin(pmax(Construct_year, 2005), 2015),
      # BonusMalus: banded, negative levels and level 0 are separate bands
      BonusMalus_banded = cut(
        BonusMalus,
        breaks = c(-Inf, -1, 0, 2, 5, 8, 11, 13, Inf),
        labels = c("<0", "0", "1-2", "3-5", "6-8", "9-11", "12-13", "14+")
      ),
      # Sum insured: increasing trend up to about 30000, little data above (in thousands)
      Sum_insured_capped = pmin(Sum_insured, 30000) / 1000,
      # Driver age: both the youngest and the oldest drivers are riskier
      D_age_banded = cut(D_age, breaks = c(-Inf, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, Inf), dig.lab = 6)
    )
}

train <- add_features(train)
valid <- add_features(valid)
```

```{r cell_11}
model_bm_band <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus_banded,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

emb_chart_plotly(model = model_bm_band, x_var = "BonusMalus_banded") |>
  show()
```

Now the fitted line follows the actual one. Banding captured a pattern
the numeric version could not.

### Adding more variables

In the same way (look at the actual vs fitted chart of a variable that
is not in the model, prepare it, add it) we add two more variables:

-   `Sum_insured` - the risk grows with the insured value up to roughly
    30 000, and there is very little exposure above, so we cap it. We
    express it in thousands, so the coefficient is easier to read.
-   `D_age` - banded into 30-and-younger, 30-40, ... 70+. (The youngest
    drivers have little exposure, so we merge them into one band.)

```{r cell_12}
model_si <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus_banded + Sum_insured_capped,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

model_age <- glm(
  data = train,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus_banded + Sum_insured_capped + D_age_banded,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)
```

```{r cell_13}
for (var_nm in get_vars(model_age)) {
  emb_chart_plotly(model = model_age, x_var = var_nm) |>
    show()
}
```

### Comparing the models

```{r cell_14}
model_list <- list(
  "1 L5 final" = model_l5,
  "2 Vehicle type" = model_veh,
  "3 + BonusMalus numeric" = model_bm_num,
  "4 + BonusMalus banded" = model_bm_band,
  "5 + Sum insured" = model_si,
  "6 + Driver age" = model_age
)

model_comparison <- compare_models(model_list, train, valid)
model_comparison
```

```{r cell_15}
model_comparison |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(train_rmse, valid_rmse), names_to = "dataset", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse, colour = dataset, group = dataset)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

How to read this table? Be careful with it:

-   The **training** RMSE falls with every sensible variable we add -
    this is expected, the model has more information to fit the data it
    sees.
-   The **validation** RMSE is what matters, but it is a noisy number:
    the validation set has only a few hundred policies with a claim, and
    the grouped RMSE is computed from just 5 groups. Differences of a few
    points between models are not reliable.
-   Notice what the validation RMSE says about **BonusMalus used as a
    number** - it is clearly the worst model, much worse than the same
    variable banded. A variable can easily hurt when it is used in the
    wrong form.

This is why the decision about a model should not rest on a single number.
We combine it with what the actual vs fitted charts show, with whether the
multipliers make business sense, and with the stability of the effects.
There is no single "correct" model - we need to be able to explain why we
chose it.

### The model for the next step

We continue with model 6: the vehicle type, BonusMalus (banded), the sum
insured (capped) and the driver age (banded). It has the lowest validation
RMSE in the table, but be honest about how much that proves: the gain over
the vehicle-type-only model is small and, with 10 groups instead of 5, it
would disappear. What really supports the choice is the following:

-   BonusMalus clearly carries the most information - the actual burning
    cost falls from about 960 to 24 across its bands and the fitted line
    follows it closely.
-   Sum insured and driver age show a weaker, noisier trend (look at the
    oldest and youngest drivers, where the fitted line overshoots) - they
    are the first candidates to drop or to merge further if we wanted a
    simpler tariff.
-   All multipliers have a direction that can be explained to a business
    partner.

In the next exercise we refit this model on all the data and turn it into
a pricing tariff.

```{r cell_16}
saveRDS(
  list(train = train, valid = valid, target_cap = target_cap),
  "/cloud/project/Data/lesson6_train_valid.rds"
)
```
